title: Angles & Parallel Lines
coreInsight: An angle measures turn or separation between rays, and intersections and parallel lines create dependable angle relationships.
targetLearnerRealization: Angle size comes from the turn between rays, not their lengths or a sketch's appearance; line structure then forces vertical, supplementary, and parallel-line angle relationships.
learningObjectives: Interpret an angle as turn between rays rather than ray length.
Use full-turn and straight-angle benchmarks of 360° and 180°.
Distinguish vertical angles from supplementary adjacent angles.
Use corresponding and alternate interior angles only when parallelism is established.
Chain angle relationships in triangles and bisected angles.

continuity.openingCallback: Estimate a turn against quarter-, half-, and full-turn benchmarks before calculating its exact degree measure.
closingSeeds: A triangle's three angles are constrained even while its shape moves.
Equal sides and equal angles can force one another in triangles.

misconceptionTargets.misconception: Angle size depends on ray length.
The drawing's appearance overrides stated relationships.
Parallel-line angle rules apply even when lines are not parallel.
Vertical and supplementary angle relationships are interchangeable.

beats.purpose: Surface the belief that longer rays make a larger angle before naming angle measure.
beats.expectedRealization: Changing ray lengths while preserving directions does not change the angle.
beats.transitionIn: Estimation compares magnitudes before exact calculation. Begin with a magnitude that records turning instead of distance.
beats.whyNow: The contrast isolates angle from length with no angle rules required.
beats.entryBridge: Track how far one direction must rotate to reach the other.
beats.exitBridge: Both pairs require the same quarter-turn even though one pair reaches farther.
learnerPrompts: Which pair requires more turning from one ray to the other?
beats.correctFeedback: Correct. Both openings are quarter-turns, so both measure 90°.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Ignore how far each ray extends and compare only their directions from the shared endpoint.

visual.ariaLabel: Short and long ray pairs sharing the same east-to-north quarter-turn

steps.title: Compare directions
steps.body: Each first ray points east and each second ray points north.

steps.title: Measure the change
steps.body: East to north is one quarter of a full turn: 360° ÷ 4 = 90°. Length never enters the calculation.

resolution.takeaway: Angle measures turn between directions, not ray length.

beats.purpose: Build 90°, 180°, and 360° from portions of one full rotation.
beats.expectedRealization: A straight angle is half a full turn and a right angle is one quarter.
beats.transitionIn: Keep the rays' lengths fixed and change only the turn.
beats.prompt: A rotating ray completes half of a full 360° turn. What angle has it swept?
beats.correctFeedback: Yes. Half of 360° is the 180° straight angle.
beats.incorrectFeedback: A half-turn uses half of 360°, not half of a right angle.

steps.title: Use the full-turn benchmark
steps.body: 360° ÷ 2 = 180°. The starting and ending rays point in opposite directions and form a straight line.

beats.purpose: Derive vertical equality and adjacent supplementation from a single intersection.
beats.expectedRealization: Opposite angles are equal, while adjacent angles sum to 180°.
beats.transitionIn: A straight line supplies 180°. Cross it with a second line and one angle determines all four.
beats.prompt: At an intersection, one angle is 68°. What are the angle directly opposite it and an angle directly beside it?
beats.correctFeedback: Correct. Vertical angles match; adjacent angles complete a straight 180°.
beats.incorrectFeedback: The opposite angle is vertical to 68°. A neighboring angle shares a straight line with it.

visual.ariaLabel: An intersection summarized by equal opposite angles and supplementary adjacent angles

steps.title: Use the opposite pair
steps.body: Rotating both boundary rays by 180° preserves their separation, so the vertical angle is 68°.

resolution.takeaway: Vertical means equal; adjacent on a line means supplementary.

beats.purpose: Make explicit that transversal shortcuts depend on parallel lines, not visual resemblance.
beats.expectedRealization: Parallel marks authorize equal corresponding and alternate interior angles; without them the inference is unsupported.
beats.transitionIn: One intersection controls four angles locally. Two intersections can share constraints only when the crossed lines have stated structure.
beats.prompt: A transversal crosses two lines. An angle at the first intersection is 117°. What extra fact guarantees the corresponding angle at the second intersection is also 117°?

options.text: The transversal is the longest segment.
The sketch makes the angles look equal.
One unrelated angle is a right angle.

beats.correctFeedback: Exactly. Parallelism is the condition that carries the angle pattern from one crossing to the other.
beats.incorrectFeedback: A diagram's appearance is not a condition. Look for the relationship between the two crossed lines.

steps.title: State the condition
steps.body: When parallel lines are cut by a transversal, corresponding angles are equal; alternate interior angles are also equal.

steps.title: Respect the boundary
steps.body: If the lines are not known to be parallel, either angle may change independently, so those equalities cannot be assumed.

resolution.takeaway: Use parallel-line angle rules only after parallelism is given or proved.

beats.purpose: Name the relationships after learners have derived their constraints.
beats.expectedRealization: Names identify which invariant or sum applies.
beats.name: Angle relationships
beats.conciseDefinition: Vertical angles are opposite at one intersection and equal. A linear pair is adjacent on a line and sums to 180°. With parallel lines, corresponding and alternate interior angles are equal.
beats.formalization: full turn = 360° · straight angle = 180° · vertical angles equal · linear pair sums to 180°
beats.memoryHook: Opposite matches; beside completes; parallel carries the pattern.

beats.purpose: Apply full-turn partitioning to a familiar central-angle model.
beats.expectedRealization: Twelve equal hour gaps split 360° into 30° sectors, and ray length is irrelevant.
beats.transitionIn: A clock packages a full turn into equal sectors. Count sectors instead of judging hand lengths.
beats.whyNow: The learner has the 360° benchmark and is ready to construct a degree measure rather than recall a clock formula.
beats.entryBridge: Find the turn per hour mark, then count the smaller gap from 10 to 12.
beats.exitBridge: Two 30° sectors make 60°; extending either hand would leave that turn unchanged.
beats.reusedRepresentation: A central pivot with two rays and a degree arc.
learnerPrompts: How many equal gaps divide the full 360° turn?
How much turn is one hour gap?
How many gaps form the smaller angle at 10:00?
Would longer hands change the result?
beats.correctFeedback: Correct. Two 30° gaps form a 60° angle.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Divide 360° by the 12 equal hour gaps, then count from 10 to 12 along the shorter route.

steps.title: Measure one gap
steps.body: The 12 equal spaces divide 360°, so each is 360° ÷ 12 = 30°.

steps.title: Count the smaller route
steps.body: From 10 to 12 spans two gaps, giving 2 × 30° = 60°.

resolution.takeaway: Equal partitions of a full turn create exact central angles.

beats.purpose: Chain equal triangle angles, an angle bisector, and a new triangle's angle sum without copying the wrong angle.
beats.expectedRealization: Each stated relationship applies to a particular pair; the requested angle belongs to a new triangle and must be recomputed.
beats.transitionIn: One relationship can determine another angle. Now several relationships must be attached to the correct vertices.
beats.whyNow: The learner can distinguish equality from supplementation and is ready to coordinate those ideas with triangle angle sum and bisection.
beats.entryBridge: Find the equal base angles, split only the named angle, then work inside triangle CRT.
beats.exitBridge: The bisected 36° is at T; angle CRT is a different angle and equals 72° by its triangle's sum.
beats.reusedRepresentation: Labeled rays whose angle constraints are tracked by location.
learnerPrompts: What are the two equal angles after the 36° apex is removed from 180°?
Why is the requested angle not automatically 36°?
What does triangle CRT's angle sum force?
beats.correctFeedback: Correct. Triangle CRT has angles 72° and 36°, so its third angle is 72°.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Keep each label at its vertex: first find the equal 72° angles, halve angle T, then use the smaller triangle's 180° sum.

steps.title: Find equal base angles
steps.body: (180° − 36°) ÷ 2 = 72°, so angles C and T of triangle CAT are each 72°.

steps.title: Apply the bisector
steps.body: TR splits the 72° angle at T into two 36° angles.

steps.title: Use the new triangle
steps.body: In triangle CRT, angle C is 72° and angle T is 36°, so angle R is 180° − 72° − 36° = 72°.

resolution.takeaway: Attach every relationship to its actual rays; a new triangle has its own angle sum.

beats.purpose: Assess vertical and supplementary angle distinctions.
beats.whyNow: Return to one intersection after the chained transfer.
beats.entryBridge: Identify whether the requested angle is opposite or adjacent.
beats.exitBridge: The location decides equality versus subtraction from 180°.
learnerPrompts: Does the requested angle share a side with 143° or sit opposite it?
beats.incorrectFeedback: Adjacent angles on a straight line sum to 180°.

beats.purpose: Assess an angle chain across parallel lines.
beats.whyNow: Use the stated parallel condition to move between intersections.
beats.entryBridge: Carry the corresponding angle, then complete a straight line.
beats.exitBridge: Parallelism gives 64° at the second crossing and supplementation gives 116°.
learnerPrompts: Which angle is copied by correspondence, and which one completes 180°?
beats.correctFeedback: Correct. The corresponding angle is 64°, so its adjacent angle is 116°.
beats.incorrectFeedback: First transfer 64° using parallelism; then subtract from 180°.

steps.title: Carry the pattern
steps.body: Corresponding angles are equal, so the matching angle is 64°.

resolution.takeaway: Parallel equality and straight-line supplementation can be chained.

beats.purpose: Assess whether learners refuse an unsupported parallel-line inference.
beats.whyNow: Remove the condition and test the boundary of the rule.
beats.entryBridge: Separate what the sketch suggests from what the statements guarantee.
beats.exitBridge: Without parallelism, the second angle is not determined.
learnerPrompts: Which fact, if any, connects the two intersections?
beats.correctFeedback: Correct. The angle cannot be determined without a parallel condition or another constraint.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Looking parallel is not the same as being stated or proved parallel.

steps.title: Audit the givens
steps.body: A transversal alone creates two unrelated intersections. No equality carries between them unless the lines are known to be parallel.

resolution.takeaway: Never borrow a parallel-line rule from appearance alone.

beats.purpose: Assess equal partitioning of a full turn at a new clock position.
beats.whyNow: Vary the number of sectors while preserving the model.
learnerPrompts: How many gaps lie on the smaller route from 4 to 12?
beats.correctFeedback: Correct. Four gaps at 30° each make 120°.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Count the smaller number of hour gaps, then multiply by 30°.

steps.title: Count and multiply
steps.body: The smaller route has four gaps, so 4 × 30° = 120°.

resolution.takeaway: Central angle equals sector count times turn per sector.

beats.purpose: Assess a multi-step triangle and exterior-angle chain.
beats.whyNow: Finish with several correctly localized relationships.
beats.entryBridge: Find the missing interior angle before its adjacent exterior angle.
beats.exitBridge: The triangle sum gives 75°, then the line gives 105°.
learnerPrompts: What does the triangle sum force before you use the straight line?
beats.correctFeedback: Correct. The third interior angle is 75°, so the adjacent exterior angle is 105°.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Subtract the two known angles from 180°, then supplement the result.

resolution.takeaway: Name the figure and relationship at each step of an angle chain.

beats.purpose: Consolidate a reliable order for angle reasoning.
beats.transitionIn: Clock sectors, intersections, parallel crossings, and triangles all became manageable once each angle was tied to a precise relationship.
beats.prompt: Which actions belong in a reliable angle routine? Select all four.

options.text: Locate whether angles are opposite, adjacent, or at separate crossings.
Check that parallelism is stated or proved before using transversal rules.
Verify straight, triangle, or full-turn sums.

response.feedback: Each action protects a different angle relationship.

beats.correctFeedback: Yes. Measure the turn, locate the relationship, check its conditions, and verify the total.
beats.incorrectFeedback: All four are needed; a sketch alone cannot replace any of them.

steps.body: Start with directions and location. Then apply only the relationship whose conditions match, and close with a 180° or 360° check when available.

resolution.takeaway: Structure determines angles; the drawing is evidence only when its relationships are stated.

beats.purpose: Create the need for triangle invariants in the next lesson.
beats.expectedRealization: A triangle may change shape while its angle sum remains fixed and equal-side conditions create further constraints.
beats.transitionIn: A fixed intersection forced local angle patterns. A triangle also keeps a global constraint while its vertices move.
beats.prompt: If one vertex of a triangle slides while the other two stay fixed, which angle quantities must change, and what total might remain unchanged?
beats.takeaway: Moving a triangle's vertex changes its angles, but not every relationship is free to change.

notes: Design: a ray-length contrast isolates turn as angle magnitude; full- and half-turn benchmarks derive straight angles; one intersection separates vertical equality from adjacency; parallel rules are introduced only with an explicit condition. The clock application partitions 360°, and the isosceles-bisector transfer coordinates several localized relationships.

Beat outline: ray-length puzzle -> turn benchmarks -> intersection families -> parallel condition -> name relationships -> authentic clock application -> authentic bisector transfer -> five independent problems -> consolidation -> moving-triangle hook.
Both mapped animations appear only after submission and their prompts follow their declared timeline states. Existing generic choice-grid visuals suffice; no renderer work was needed.

Generated answers were recomputed using turn partitions, 180° sums, correspondence under stated parallelism, and independent reverse-sum or option audits. The lesson remains draft pending human review.
